name: American stoneware crock
region: New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Ohio and Vermont, United States
summary: Straight-sided stoneware for the farm and the dairy: crocks, churns, jugs and jars. A salt or slip glaze makes the wall tight, and a swift cobalt motif marks the size.

philosophy.core_thesis: A crock must hold butter, pickles or pork for a winter, so the body is dense stoneware and the only ornament is one quick blue brush stroke.
design_principles: Throw a straight-sided crock with a wall 10 to 14 mm thick; the weight resists frost and knocks.
Add two ear handles or a ring of lugs, 4 cm below the rim, to lift a 10-litre pot.
Mark the volume in gallons on the front: stamp or brush the number, 1 to 6.
Brush one cobalt motif, a bird, a flower or a leaf, in a few strokes of slip; the stroke blurs a little in the fire.
Glaze the pot with salt, or dip it in a brown Albany slip.
Fire the pots at 1200 to 1250 °C in a groundhog or beehive kiln, and throw salt at the peak.
Keep the rim plain and flat, so that a cloth and a stone fit on top.
anti_patterns: A decal or a printed label

form.shape: Straight-sided crocks, ovoid jugs, churns, preserving jars and bean pots in sizes of 1 to 6 gallons.
form.profile: A tall cylinder that swells a little at the shoulder; a jug has a round shoulder and a narrow neck with a loop handle.
form.foot_and_rim: A flat base with a sharp edge; a plain flat rim, thick enough for a lid or a cloth cover.
form.proportion: Height 20 to 45 cm; width about two thirds of the height; wall 10 to 14 mm.
rules: Keep the wall straight and the rim flat, so that a plate sits on top.
Fix ear handles near the rim.
Put the volume mark and one motif on the front, in the upper half.

bodies.rule: Use a grey or buff stoneware of local clay that vitrifies at 1200 °C and does not leak. Keep fine white bodies out: the pot is heavy and plain by design.

methods: throwing on the wheel in large lumps of 5 to 20 kg
wire-cutting the base from the wheel
forming.joins: Ear handles and lugs are made as a coil and luted with slip; a jug handle is pulled in one stroke and bent in a loop.
forming.details: A visible throwing spiral on the wall, a thin blue smear at the edge of the brush, and a flat spot where the pot rested in the kiln.

glaze.pattern: One cobalt bird, flower, leaf or swag on the front, a large number for the size, and sometimes a line of incised waves round the shoulder.
glaze.gloss: Salt glaze is a satin skin of 20 to 40 GU; brown Albany slip is a glossy dark coat of 50 to 70 GU.
glaze.wear: The glaze is hard and does not wear; the body shows a grey or tan chip at the rim.

palette.strategy: A plain ground of grey, tan or brown with one strong blue; the cobalt is the only bright colour.

firing.kiln: A beehive or groundhog kiln fired with wood or coal; salt is thrown at the top of the firing.
firing.scale: Hundreds of potteries along the Hudson, in New Jersey and in Ohio; the ware was cheap and sold by the gallon.
firing.signs: A stamped gallon number, a blue brush stroke with a soft blur, and an orange-peel skin on the salt glaze.

emotion.target_response: A sturdy farm-kitchen comfort: the viewer sees a heavy grey pot with one blue bird and thinks of a pantry and a hard winter.

use_cases: a farmhouse or an antique-shop set dressing
a museum label on 19th-century American stoneware
a brief for a rustic utensil crock with one blue motif
avoid_when: the brief needs a white body
the brief needs a thin wall
the brief needs an oven dish

modifiers.how: Change to a glass-ceramic body with a smooth white surface and a printed decal.
Make the form a round-bellied jug with a sprigged mask and a grey-brown salt glaze.

wall_thickness.note: A crock wall is 10 to 14 mm so that it resists frost and knocks.
